articles.title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
articles.description: The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so . Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine. The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. A less apoplectic strain of the same underlying sentiment holds that President Trump’s willingness to meet his Russian and Chinese counterparts is in itself an unnecessary concession to Russia and China that merely signals weakness and does nothing to advance U.S. interests; as if the avoidance of nuclear war with China were not a vital U.S. interest. articles.description: Soros-Backed Kim Gardner Used Public Money To Pay For Her Last Ethics Scandal. The court reprimanded her, fined her $750 and ordered her to pay the costs of the disciplinary case. articles.description: A Tonne Of Dead Fish Tossed Overboard Every Five Minutes As Big UK Trawlers Dodge Fines Fishing boats are throwing more than 100,000 tonnes of fish a year back into UK waters, roughly a tonne every five minutes, in breach of rules that have required them to land their whole catch since 2019 , according to a new report from the marine conservation charity Oceana UK. Hugo Tagholm, the group's chief executive, wrote that the haul discarded from UK quota stocks last year comes to about a quarter of the seafood British shoppers buy from supermarkets and large retailers in a year. The report, titled "Catch Me If You Can," says the dumping happens when crews start hauling more valuable species and tip the cheaper fish already in the hold over the side. Tagholm told The Telegraph that "all sea life is valuable. It's really shocking." Data obtained by Oceana show that vessels over 12 metres broke fisheries rules during 66% of at-sea inspections in English waters in the year to March 2026, against about 10% for boats under 10 metres. articles.description: Europe's Demographic Crisis: Share Of Households With Children Drops To Record-Low 23.3% Authored by Remix News Staff via Remix News , The share of European Union households that include at least one person under the age of 18 has fallen to 23.3 percent, the lowest level recorded in the Eurostat statistical figures that began in 2010. The latest figures, released on Nov. 20 and obtained from the EU Labour Force Survey, confirm that the share of family households has fallen steadily for 15 years while the share of adults living alone has only grown . In 2010, households with children still accounted for 26.9 percent of the EU total. The proportion slipped to 25.9 percent in 2015 and 25 percent in 2020 before reaching 23.3 percent in 2025. Over the same span, the share of single-adult households without children rose from 33.6 percent in 2015 to 37.5 percent in 2025. Now, the category of people living alone is the single largest household category in the entire EU. Households with both parents and a child make up an even smaller share, accounting for only 14.7 percent in 2025, falling from 16.6 percent in 2015. Single-parent households remain at only 3 percent. articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

Within a few minutes, you find just the right one, in the colour you want and at a huge discount. articles.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
articles.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
articles.description: Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff. Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. Continue reading...

articles.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
articles.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
articles.description: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the

articles.title: Houseplant hacks: does grouping plants together increase humidity?
articles.description: It will help during winter months, but there are better solutions for really thirsty plants The problem With the onset of winter, the heating comes on, humidity drops and tropical plants that yearn for rainforest conditions end up in something closer to a desert. Cue crispy leaf edges. Humidifiers work, but they require buying, filling and cleaning. Misting works, but you need to remember to do it. So, a free, lazy alternative has an obvious appeal. The hack This hack is based on transpiration. Plants constantly release water vapour through their leaves, so huddling them together raises the humidity around them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: A close watch on this autumn’s leaf fall – it’s been unpredictable | Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
articles.description: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
articles.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s

Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
articles.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Working with Kanye West? Talk about intractable egos!’ Caroline Shaw: the Pulitzer-winning composer everyone wants to work with
articles.description: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no ot

articles.title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story
articles.description: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laurea

articles.title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love
articles.description: Save money and help the planet with these genuine discounts on everything from bamboo toilet paper to B Corp-certified bedding • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals at independent retailers Ethical and sustainable probably aren’t the first words that spring to mind when you think of Black Friday. The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. Many of our Filter recommendations tick either the green box or the affordable box, but we (and you, I expect) would be a lot happier if more of them ticked both. Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: at 31 I felt I was running out of time – then my 83-year-old grandma got a tattoo
articles.description: With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong … It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Budapest in winter: ‘Gloomy days call for a plunge in one of the city’s ornate bathhouses’
articles.description: A neighbourhood that transforms into a living advent calendar, hot chocolate beneath chandeliers and 16th-century baths – Hungary’s capital is full of winter warmth Each December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. Continue reading...

articles.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
articles.description: People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found. The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
articles.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. If this sounds like a kids’ party from hell, blame me, because it’s actual

articles.title: Stick or switch? UK billpayers weigh up how to beat January energy jump
articles.description: Despite dozens of fixed deals lower than next Ofgem price cap, many customers argue savings do not justify the risk Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January “I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing charge,” says Andy, who lives on Scotland’s west coast. “I have an electric vehicle and an air-source heat pump and use a lot of off-peak energy. I’d like to stay with Octopus Energy … but there are better-looking deals out there.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave
articles.description: White Cube Bermondsey, London Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla , after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the ca

articles.title: Ten years on … the Bad Boys of Brexit are back in town | John Crace
articles.description: It feels as if we’re destined to hold the same referendum every decade. Nige, Arron and co are up for the fight Roll back the years. The Bad Boys of Brexit have reformed and are back in town. Andy Wigmore on comms. Arron Banks on lead vocals and money. Nigel Farage on doing whatever the hell he likes. Apart from spending his own cash on security. This time round, though, a woman has joined the band. Step forward, Catherine McBride. Probably the only woman alive who Nige thinks he can trust not to be totally pissed by 3pm. Even so, you can sense that this is a relationship destined to end in tears. Give it a couple of months and Catherine will be wishing she had never met Nige and Arron. Continue reading...

articles.title: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
articles.description: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak , which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating . Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack
articles.description: (Atlantic) Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits. Continue read

articles.title: Is grandma asking rude questions at the dinner table again? This Instagram account can help
articles.description: Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? When are you going to have kids? – punctuated by unnerving thrusts of her steak knife. The granddaughter is clearly uncomfortable, but her grandmother pays no attention. Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
articles.description: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. articles.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
articles.description: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. articles.title: Cop31 collapse must be a catalyst for genuine climate action | Letters
articles.description: Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire ( A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

articles.title: The British Library is wrong to repurpose its reading rooms | Letters
articles.description: To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as ‘evidence’ is unworthy of our world-class research institution, says Marcia Saunders After a cyber-attack in 2023 , which Ciaran Martin, a former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, described as “ one of the worst cyber incidents in British history ”, use of the British Library’s reading rooms fell dramatically ( British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces, 20 November ). Throughout 2024-25, services were heavily affected, including archives, manuscripts, books and online journal articles. All readers’ tickets were suspended and initially were reissued for limited periods of time. It should surprise no one that use of the reading rooms fell off. Only last month was access to the UK web archive (partially) restored. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Labour party has lost the plot on net zero | Letters
articles.description: Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh Watching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero ( Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November ) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war. Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies , which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry. Continue reading...

articles.title: London Museum’s donors and the capital’s dubious domination | Letters
articles.description: Omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that ‘magisterial’ civic amenities just happen by magic, writes Beth Breeze . Plus letters from Rendel Harris and Tom Uprichard Oliver Wainwright’s extremely positive review of the “magisterial” new London Museum will encourage many to visit ( Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight, 24 November ). But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. In particular, omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that fantastic civic amenities just happen by magic, or are totally funded by taxpayers. Continue reading...

articles.title: Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election?
articles.description: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro , an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation. “Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.” Continue reading...

articles.title: How datacentres are driving an illegal mining rush in the Amazon ‘more devastating than gold’
articles.description: As demand for tin ores pushes up prices, criminal gangs are exploiting Indigenous lands and weak regulation to profit from Brazil’s abundant cassiterite While searching for documents tied to an illegal cassiterite export network last September, Brazilian federal police officers were surprised to find a link between an illegal mining and money-laundering scheme and an address connected to one of Brazil ’s biggest showbusiness stars from the 90s. Alexandre Pires, a popular pagode singer-songwriter, is now under investigation as part of Operation Disco de Ouro (Gold Disc) for his alleged involvement in a scheme to illegally ship cassiterite worth millions of dollars abroad. During the investigation, police uncovered a message in which his agent, Matheus Possebon, allegedly admitted to his participation and said that he failed to deliver the illegal ore he had promised his associates. articles.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
articles.description: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our ho

articles.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
articles.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, an

articles.title: The 4thWrite short story prize winner – a tale of teenage girlhood
articles.description: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity

articles.title: Indelible art: the punk tattoo artist preserving an ancient Thai tradition – in pictures
articles.description: When Aod-Sarawut Waewngam learned tattooing at the age of 18, his goal was to tattoo himself. Drawn to punk culture as a teenager, he first saw the art as an act of rebellion. But, as his skill grew, he developed an interest in traditional Thai tattoos. Now he is one of the few to have mastered the ancient art of Lanna leg tattoos, which cover the wearer from the knees to the waist, and is working to preserve the traditional art form while adapting the practice to modern times Photography by Wissarut Weerasopon ‘It opens up doors and minds’: inside Sydney’s tattoo convention Continue reading...

articles.title: How to turn leftover porridge into brilliant cookies – recipe | Waste not
articles.description: Upcycle the scrapings from your porridge pot into delicious and nutritious oaty snacks featuring store-cupboard seeds and dried fruit, too My hope is that today’s recipe will inspire you to save that little bit of cooked porridge left in a bowl and to upcycle it into these wonderful cookies. The porridge acts as the binder, rather than the usual egg, which saves money and keeps things vegan and accessible. If you don’t have leftover porridge, don’t fret – a brown banana will also do the trick. Flaxseeds are a worthy addition – they help improve the integrity of the cookie and add omega 3 and 6 – but they’re not essential. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Nobody showed up but me’: will Friendsgiving survive gen Z?
articles.description: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.description: Exclusive: Analysis gives most detailed picture yet of the nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022 Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war Alexander Korepanov signed up to fight in August 2023. He was wounded twice and twice sent back to the front. On 11 May 2025, after 20 months at war, he was killed in the village of Uspenovka, near the eastern Ukrainian city of Pokrovsk, aged 52. More than 5,000 died with him that week. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Big names are notoriously flighty’: will Gordon Ramsay save Top Gear – and can he handle the drudgery?
articles.description: He may be a proud petrolhead with a racing licence … but superstars have been lured in before then flounced off. The BBC simply can’t afford for that to happen again There is a lot riding on 2028’s Top Gear revival. Ever since The Punch That Changed Everything, the series has ostensibly remained the BBC’s landmark motoring show, even though several successive iterations have demonstrably been nothing of the sort. But hope springs eternal, and this time the BBC seems to be pinning everything it’s got on Gordon Ramsay. And, look, let’s get the bad stuff out of the way first. At first glance this looks very much like the BBC has done another Joey. Ramsay is a huge name. Famous, wealthy, instantly recognisable and with global appeal, he has the potential to open Top Gear up to a brand new audience. Continue reading...

articles.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
articles.description: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?
articles.description: Backed by the KLF, a monument is being built using 34,592 bricks, each containing a deceased person’s glazed ashes. Is this the future of funerals? We join emotional marchers on Birkenhead’s smoky, noisy Day of the Dead Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people. “My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA

articles.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
articles.description: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy Continue reading...

articles.title: The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon
articles.description: Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes. It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He aske

articles.title: Neville, Carragher and the inescapable podcasting feedback loop of doom | Jonathan Liew
articles.description: Even the best managers can struggle to escape ex-players’ need to manufacture a crisis for content. Enter Michael Carrick … A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick. Neville: Just so you know, we’re already filming. This is the intro bit, where we show everyone coming on to set and doing some light banter. It humanises us. The viewer sees it and thinks we’re just mates chatting about football, rather than scions of a global podcast empire commercially obliged to produce an endless scroll of provocative content for money. I always say: why can’t you be both? Continue reading...

articles.description: Exclusive: Frontbenchers join scores of party colleagues urging Burnham not to let ministers approve project Opinion: Why Labour MPs are opposing Rosebank Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs – including a handful of frontbenchers – writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project. Ninety-two backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers have signed a letter to Andy Burnham urging him not to let his ministers approve the scheme for the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters. articles.title: Mandelson tried to set up meeting between Trump adviser and lobbying firm he held shares in
articles.description: Then ambassador to US wanted to discuss alternatives to World Trade Organization in ‘under the radar’ meeting, documents reveal UK politics live – latest updates Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting between an economic adviser to Donald Trump and a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, while he still held shares in the company, newly released documents reveal. In April 2025, while ambassador to Washington, Mandelson wanted to hold a lunch to discuss “alternative options” to the World Trade Organization and on how “like-minded partners come to terms with China and its practices”. He told the economic adviser he wanted to bring “a former trade colleague of mine” with “interesting views” who could “lead off”. He added: “It would be best to keep this under the radar”. Continue reading...

articles.description: Latest figure of young people not in education, employment or training remains close to highest level in a decade Business live – latest updates UK politics live – latest updates The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) has decreased but remains close to a million as Andy Burnham’s government pushes to tackle Britain’s youth jobs crisis. articles.description: People’s party alters video of PM putting on Lamine Yamal’s Spain shirt in latest contentious use of AI in election race Spanning 17 seconds, the campaign video showed the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking to the camera as he put on the jersey of the national football team. “Because this is what Spain is: a pluralistic and diverse country,” he said as he turned to reveal the number 19 on his back – the shirt number of the star player Lamine Yamal. articles.description: Kyiv’s destruction of the road section of the Crimean Bridge has left drivers facing hazardous journeys through occupied southern Ukraine Russians once packed their swimming trunks and sunscreen for summer holidays in Crimea, or hiking boots for trips in the colder months to the picturesque Black Sea peninsula annexed by Vladimir Putin in 2014. articles.title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’
articles.description: Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found. The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules. Continue reading...

articles.description: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid? It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association. Continue reading...

articles.title: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’
articles.description: As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear You ’ ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJax No. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus. What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and imp

articles.title: I spent 69 hours building Lego – here are the best sets for Christmas
articles.description: From Bluey and KPop Demon Hunters to Star Wars, Hogwarts and a working pinball machine, there’s a build to delight everyone • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 Lego may have been around for almost a hundred years, but it’s as popular as ever. Don’t take our word for it: we asked kids , teens and tweens what they wanted for Christmas this year, and Lego made it on to every single list. But with a range of collaborations with Star Wars, Harry Potter and other classic nerdy franchises, there’s plenty for (not so) grownups to get excited about as well. So when I was asked to try out some of Lego’s latest and most exciting launches, I jumped at the chance. I’ve spent the last few months turning my flat into my own personal Legoland. I built set after set until my fingers were sore and my patience thin (69hrs 31mins in total), all in the name of finding the best sets for all ages. From KPop Demon Hunters to Lando Norris’s helmet and even a retro-style pinball machine, here are the best Lego gifts for 2026. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
articles.description: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!” Continue reading...

articles.title: Sinister signs, suicidal shepherds and a sensational six-hour song: Ragnar Kjartansson’s art is heroically human
articles.description: Goodwood Art Foundation The Icelandic artist’s enigmatic monuments, melancholic landscape paintings and never-ending love song are witty, moving and ravishingly conceptual Live in the gallery a man in a dark suit and white shoes leans cabaret-style against a piano and sings about his one great love. “Jenny kissed me,” he intones in a voice both melodic and casually conversational. He croons the words of this love song again, and again, and again. Icelandic artist Ragnar Kjartansson’s durational performance (which means it takes a heck of a long time) is beguiling and beautiful. It’s also a brilliant interpretation of a small masterpiece of English Romantic poetry, Jenny Kiss’d Me, by Leigh Hunt : “Jenny kissed me when we met / Jumping from the chair she sat in.” The poet demands that “Time, you thief” write this down so that he can keep this memory of a perfect moment of love. Continue reading...

articles.title: I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating? | Leading questions
articles.description: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. articles.title: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago
articles.description: Bournemouth International Centre Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer. Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC we

articles.title: Where does the pope do his big shop?​ And is he buying white beans this week?
articles.description: ​I set out to visit the supermarket in Vatican City and discovered who can actually shop there and what they might be cooking A couple of years ago, it was announced that the supermarket inside Vatican City was to be taken over by the Gabrielli group and become one of their medium-sized Tigre stores “known for daily freshness and a welcoming and courteous atmosphere”. I remember reading this announcement in Roma Today and assuming the new supermarket would be like the impeccably efficient Vatican post office and open to everyone, and that one day I would share a freezer aisle with cardinals, nuns and off-duty Swiss Guards. Fast forward two years to the Feast team’s discovery that Vatican City is one of two countries in which there are no Feast app users (the other is North Korea). “What do they eat in Vatican City?” was the next question. Bingo, I thought, knowing exactly where Vatican residents do at least some of their shopping. Here was my chance to shop and to investigate, and to see if the special offers at our local Tigre are the same as in Papa Leo XIV’s hood in Vatican City, the smallest independent state in the world. Continue reading...

articles.title: Young people are having less sex. What's going on? - video
articles.description: Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse. To unpick some of the possible reasons behind these declines, Madeleine Finlay hears from science editor and co-host Ian Sample. He tells her why young people might be having sex later, and what could account for the striking rise in women reporting that they don’t want children. Continue reading...

articles.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes
articles.description: Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills , just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK . The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains. Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Continue reading...

articles.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
articles.description: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we ha

articles.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
articles.description: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers Continue reading...

articles.title: The worst thing about winter isn’t the cold … it’s the noise | Adrian Chiles
articles.description: Sitting in a pub, the doors closed against the freezing weather, my friend and I could barely hear each other over the cacophony of chatter There’s one aspect of winter that, in a crowded field, I find most unbearable. Not the darkness, the wetness, the greyness or the cold. Miserable, all of them, but these I can deal with, just about. What I really can’t bear is the noise. It was only last night that this dawned on me. I met a friend in a pub. Over the long, too hot summer, we’d sit in the garden, which obviously isn’t possible just now. So we sat inside, which was fine other than the fact that we each heard barely half of what the other had to say. Because when winter comes doors are closed and all the noise is shut inside with nowhere to go. The pub wasn’t even that busy, but, in this closed environment, devoid of anything so crass as soft furnishings, it doesn’t take much for quiet chatter to turn into a nerve-shredding tinnitus-inducing cacophony. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Danish prime minister’s coarse language about migrants has no place in the EU | Shada Islam
articles.description: Mette Frederiksen’s ‘great replacement’ remarks shows how centrist EU leaders have normalised previously shocking ideas With the notable exception of Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who may soon be out of office, EU leaders appear most united when promoting one clear aim: reinforcing the already heavily guarded borders of Fortress Europe against unwanted migrants. Policymakers who once criticised Donald Trump’s immigration policies as inhumane now enact measures that increasingly resemble Washington’s ugly playbook of ICE home raids, family separations, deportations and offshore detention deals. Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory company Continue reading...

articles.title: Two teams face Nations Championship relegation under 2030 playoff plans

The Guardian has learned that the favoured mechanism for introducing relegation is for the bottom sides in both the northern and southern hemisphere tables to face a one-legged playoff match against the winners of the equivalent tables in the tier two Nations Cup, which is run by World Rugby. Continue reading...

articles.title: Human flamethrower Aaron Rodgers lays bare the cultural rot at the once-great Steelers
articles.description: The quarterback’s spectacularly messy exit from Pittsburgh could herald an overdue collapse at one of the NFL’s most famous franchises Nobody in the world, except maybe Pittsburgh Steelers owner Art Rooney II, is surprised that the franchise’s marriage of convenience with Aaron Rodgers ended in spectacular flames . Despite their own elevated idea of themselves, Pittsburgh have been one of the NFL’s messiest soap operas for a solid decade. When they linked up with the league’s messiest quarterback, it seemed certain we would get … even more mess. When they doubled down last offseason by hiring the coach with whom Rodgers had fallen out in Green Bay in the late 2010s, the mess became inevitable. We’d seen hints of the approaching drama in the season’s first 11 weeks. “What the fuck … call it!” Rodgers yelled at McCarthy as he looked for a play in early October. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pochettino claims officials ‘punished’ Manchester United in chaotic Sporting draw
articles.description: Head coach questions ‘difficult to understand’ decisions Zirkzee joins Pochettino in offering support to Lammens Mauricio Pochettino claimed Manchester United were punished unfairly after again appearing to suffer from faulty officiating in Wednesday night’s 2-2 draw at Sporting . The key decision from Szymon Marciniak came when Amad Diallo’s first-half strike was ruled out due to the referee adjudging Youri Tielemans to have fouled Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish. The women’s football team were playing Germany in the World Cup final. TV4 set a new viewing record as almost half the nation watched the game go into extra time, where Nia Künzer scored the golden goal winner after 98 minutes. It was a bitter pill to swallow but there was still the belief that the tournament would mark the start of women’s football’s commercial breakthrough in Sweden. articles.title: Amanda Seyfried needed ‘five-factor authentication’ to read You Can See Everything script but still ‘told everyone’
articles.description: Actor who had played fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in TV drama The Dropout reveals how she was drafted in to the hit documentary ‘at the last minute’ Amanda Seyfried says that the script and footage of You Can See Everything was kept secret even from her until the last possible moment, and that despite being asked not to reveal her involvement in the project she “told a lot of people”. Seyfried was speaking on the Jimmy Fallon Show on Tuesday, after the film’s extraordinary commercial success in North America , where it is already the third most successful documentary in box office history. articles.title: Contraceptive pill usage in Great Britain fell drastically in last decade, research finds

New findings from the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), published in The Lancet, found that almost one in five women in Great Britain at risk of unintended pregnancy were not using effective contraception.
