articles.title: Novelist’s first album in eight years has Skepta, skits and soul – and showcases a true British original
articles.description: ( Mashwrks) Sharp, unsentimental rhymes and a fearless disregard for genre make Scenes a richly varied victory lap for for one of grime’s most distinctive talents It’s not often that a UK rap album arrives accompanied by its own air freshener and video game, but here we are. Head over to Novelist’s website, and you can find not merely the usual means of promoting a new release – branded hoodies, T-shirts and so on – but a scented mirror hanger that bears the album’s artwork and Scenes: the Drive, a vaguely Mario Kart-ish arcade game that involves driving around the landmarks of London and Los Angeles avoiding buses and the attentions of the traffic police to the strains of an album track called Prime. But then, from the moment he appeared on the grime scene in his teens – so young he now constitutes an elder statesman in his late 20s – the south Londoner has cut something of a maverick figure in the world of UK rap. He arrived bearing a moniker that seemed oddly bookish among his more grittily named peers. His early releases saw him working alongside defiantly left-field producer Mumdance. He attracted a lot of press attention of the “grime’s brightest new hope” variety, but seemed

articles.title: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice
articles.description: The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law “Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was bor

articles.title: TV tonight: Ella Purnell returns as serial killer Sweetpea
articles.description: The dark comedy is back with a Rhiannon getting into deeper trouble. Plus: the terrifying truth about sinkholes. Here’s what to watch this evening 9pm, Sky Atlantic Things are looking up for Ella Purnell’s casually murderous Rhiannon Lewis as the dark comedy returns. Junior cop Marina has been warned to stay off her trail. And new office arrival Freya (Taj Atwal) seems much more sympathetic to her ideas. Now, there’s just the awkward problem of a body to dispose of. Purnell is just the right mix of sullen and vulnerable but Sweetpea struggles to find its tone: a drama about a serial killer should be more dynamic than this. Phil Harrison Continue reading...

articles.title: Tulisa: The Reckoning review – it’s hard to believe how far the disgusting drugs set-up went
articles.description: The star was chewed up and spewed out by the tabloids after the Sun on Sunday sting in 2013. But she is disarming in this fight for change – and ready to ‘raise a bit of hell’ In 2011, Tulisa Contostavlos was at the peak of her powers. At 22, the N-Dubz singer turned solo artist had landed a coveted position as a judge on The X Factor, stepping into Cheryl Cole’s towering stilettos. As she puts it here, her pitch to X Factor supremo Simon Cowell was simple: “You’re gonna need someone to sit there and look pretty and cry when [there are] emotional moments, and you’re gonna need someone to tell people they’re rubbish when they’re rubbish – and I’m gonna do both.” Cowell hired her on the spot, she says. Tulisa was a household name, but sections of the British media treated her with contempt, with headlines that played up her working-class background and labelled her a chav. Much of this three-part series is concentrated, however, on the most egregious example of the press turning on her: a sting by the Sun on Sunday in 2013, which saw Tulisa groomed into believing she was auditioning for a Hollywood film over the course of several months. Eventually, she was asked to supply drugs to a

articles.title: Tonight the Music Seems So Loud by Sathnam Sanghera audiobook review – in praise of George Michael
articles.description: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singer When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess. This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders). Continue reading...

articles.title: Lumière album review – finding solace in the rich, lyrical world of French cello music
articles.description: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasionally the cello line feels as if it could use more breath, more space in which to ask questions. There’s a sense of security in that sustained tone, though, and it serves the consolatory aspect of the p

articles.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power
articles.description: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...

articles.description: Need a break from all the crime and violence? There are plenty of places to get away from it all in Leonida As Leonida goes, Mount Kalaga is the top of the world. articles.title: Dressmaker review – delightful business sim is a cut above
articles.description: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. An outfit for the office? A pencil skirt is a good call. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bring me the scrotum stapler! Is this the world’s most extreme performance artist?
articles.description: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.title: O come, all ye faithful! Why theatres are bringing audiences on stage, from Jesus Christ Superstar to Cloud 9
articles.description: A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors at the heart of the action. What are the risks and rewards? In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. We feel the energy of the ensemble’s dance moves, seem to join the crowd of Jesus’s followers – and those who conspire against him – and come extraordinarily close to the musical’s star, Sam Ryder, who rests right by my feet after his solo Gethsemane. It’s as close as I’ve been to the beating heart of a big West End production. Until, that is, the following week when I watch the captivating revival of Rent at the Tom Stoppard theatre from o

articles.title: ‘When I cut these women out I feel like I’m freeing them’: the feminist collage artists taking scissors to the patriarchy
articles.description: A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto. The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share

articles.title: I’ve been covering Black Friday deals for seven years – here are the rules that stop me from overspending
articles.description: Arm yourself with a list, learn how to spot a genuinely good deal and don’t give in to Fomo to shop smarter this season • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops this Black Friday I’ve been writing about Black Friday deals since 2019, and while you may think spending hours scrolling online retailers’ deals would turn me into a shopping addict, it has (fortunately) done the opposite. Retailers know that, for many of us, this is the time of year we finally buy that hefty investment we’ve been debating, or else blitz through the kids’ letter to Santa. If you play your cards right, it’s an excellent way to save cash. I’d like to think I’ve got my shopping strategy down to a fine art, so here’s how I make Black Friday work for me. Make sure you go in with the right mindset. Relentless discounts and non-stop advertising are designed to make you feel frenzied. When I panic that something will sell out and feel myself rushing to buy it, I find it helpful to close my browser, take a breather, and remember that retailers need my custom more than I need that new coat. Continue reading...

articles.description: Having built its reputation on big, brash reds, the centre of US winemaking is keeping pace with changing tastes and now becoming known for crisp whites, too I was always more of a Dawson’s Creek girlie than a fan of The OC , yet the subject of this column has found me wrestling with the earworm that is the latter’s theme tune : “California, here we come/Right back where we started from.” For Scribe Winery , at the southern end of the Sonoma Valley, this is apt, though I’m not sure winemaker Andrew Mariani would thank me for the comparison. Since buying 100 hectares here in 2007, he and his brother, Adam, have been restoring the land to viticulture after an interlude as a turkey farm. Some of the Marianis’ vines are riesling and sylvaner, honouring the German immigrant family who first cultivated them here in the 1850s, but they make up a small proportion of Scribe’s production, which is focused on bright, bracing chardonnay and terroir-driven pinot noir. It’s an approach that reflects the trend of drinkers turning away from the beefy reds, particularly cabernet sauvignon, that made California famous, towards fresher – dare I say Old World? – styles. articles.title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
articles.description: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. articles.description: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Aix-en-Provence in winter: sweet treats and people watching in the quintessential Provençal city
articles.description: Market stalls are laden with local delicacies in the run-up to Christmas, while the city’s elegant cafes make the perfect spot to sit and watch the world go by Famous for its fabulous fruit and vegetable markets, Aix-en-Provence extends its stalls in winter to include les treize desserts de Noël , the 13 desserts of a traditional Provençal Christmas. I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. The delay gave competitors a little extra time to stretch and practise. Coaches paraded up and down the line, giving some last-minute advice on strategy and technique to the waiting men and women facing down their targets. Pavlo and Vadym share a laugh during the laser tag trials. Pavlo lost his left leg from a landmine in 2023 and swimming became his path to physical and mental recovery. articles.title: Belfast Flood Alleviation Scheme Sept 14-18
articles.description: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme Training Exercise A training exercise to install the temporary defences will take place between 14 – 18 September 2026. This year the locations are: Harbour Estate Sydenham (Greggs Quay to The O2 Belfast) Sydenham (Pottinger's Quay) Ravenhill As part of the exercise, the slip road from Ravenhill Road to the Albert Bridge will be closed overnight between 11pm and 6am on Wednesday 16 September. If required , the closure may also be in place on Thursday 17 September again overnight between 11pm and 6am. Diversion signage will be provided, directing city centre-bound traffic via Bridge End and Queen's Bridge. There may also be some short-term disruption and temporary footpath closures at other locations. Advisory signs will be provided where necessary, including along the towpath. The Department would like to thank the public in advance for their patience. Further details, including locations and programme, are available at: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme | Department for Infrastructure .

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.description: Since returning to the White House, President Donald Trump has increasingly relied on special envoys to deal with some of his most vexing foreign policy challenges. While Trump slashed the use of special envoys in his first term, he has come around in his second term, in part because they allow him to bypass his career foreign service officers by compartmentalizing information from “deep state bureaucrats” who he has accused of spying on him and leaking his dealmaking to the press. As in previous administrations, the current Trump administration has assembled a collection of envoys largely based on region and policy imperative. Regions like the Middle East, South and Central Asia, and the Arctic all have special envoys, as do specific countries like Syria, Belarus, Greenland, and Ukraine (currently vacant). Similarly high-profile or strategic policy objectives like hostage affairs and combating anti-Semitism also have designated special envoys. But where the Trump Administration deviates from his predecessors is in Africa. articles.description: One Of America's Most Famous Whiskey Distilleries Is Staying Dark Indefinitely Jim Beam won't restart distilling at its flagship James B. Beam distillery in Clermont, Kentucky next year, and the Suntory-owned bourbon brand won't say when the stills there will run again . When the company announced the shutdown last December, it was billed as a one-year pause covering 2026, with distilling at the historic campus set to resume in 2027. Now a company spokesperson has declined to give Food Dive any new timeline, saying only that Jim Beam will "reassess production needs as our forecasts evolve." Jim Beam production has moved to the Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, the brand's largest, capable of 45 million original proof gallons a year . The Clermont site stays open for tastings, warehousing and bottling, and its smaller Fred B. Noe craft distillery keeps making Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's. No layoffs have been tied to the pause, and the company says it will use the downtime for infrastructure upgrades. (Nov 18), taxes on labor generate about two-thirds of federal revenue, and once you add individual income taxes on things like dividends and capital gains, individual income and payroll taxes accounted for 84% of everything the government collected in 2024 . Six days earlier Jensen Huang was out as chief executive of Nvidia, the company he co-founded, in what I call a coup. articles.title: Sorry, But You Can't Park There
articles.description: Sorry, But You Can't Park There An Amazon Prime Air delivery drone crashed onto the roof of a home in Huntington Woods this week, a neighborhood located about 15 miles northwest of downtown Detroit.  The Detroit Free Press reported that the 80-pound MK30 commercial delivery drone had just delivered a bottle of shampoo to a customer when it struck a fiber-optic cable, spiraled out of control, became entangled in a power line, and landed on a nearby garage. Amazon spokesman Jack Stelzner confirmed that a drone had landed on a resident's "shed," describing such incidents as extremely rare . "Anytime a delivery does not go as planned, we investigate what happened ," Stelzner said. He didn't say whether Amazon would halt service in the area following the crash.  The local outlet said the National Transportation Safety Board is gathering information about the incident and has yet to say whether it will open an investigation.  Officials remove an Amazon delivery drone from a Huntington Woods garage roof in the first known crash in metro Detroit. articles.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
articles.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. articles.title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon
articles.description: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . Continue reading...

articles.title: United Strings of Europe review – they’re the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz
articles.description: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
articles.description: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. articles.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested
articles.description: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. articles.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures

Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, th

articles.title: Puzzles and games are finally all in one place
articles.description: The latest updates on our trivia, logic, word and number games, as explained by our new octopod mascot, Ink The Guardian finally has an online home for its puzzles and games , to go with the dedicated puzzles section in our app. We’re planning to expand the number of puzzles we offer over the coming weeks and months, with more trivia, logic, word and number games in the works. Here to explain the changes is Ink , an octopus who has just started his new role as the Guardian’s puzzles and games mascot. Hand instructions to actors (6) Shopper set out – female with a good idea of what is in store (10) Continue reading...

articles.title: Caffeine has crept into everything. With all the buzz, are we at risk of too much of a high? | Antiviral
articles.description: We are offered a seemingly endless array of drinks and foods that now come with the world’s most consumed psychoactive drug Read more in the Antiviral series Feeling tired and need a pick-me-up but finding your morning cup of coffee isn’t touching the sides? Instead of the predictable choice (a second coffee), you could instead opt for a seemingly endless array of other drinks and foods that now come with added caffeine. You might energise yourself before your morning gym session with a few caffeinated scoops of a pre-workout supplement. Afterwards, you could refuel with a caffeinated protein shake or a protein bar with added guarana – whose seeds contain caffeine. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
articles.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . Continue reading...

articles.title: Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to?
articles.description: The digital butler, which can go shopping on behalf of users, is available in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. What do you think about it? Meta is continuing its rollout of its Muse AI assistant, with the UK the latest country where the digital butler will be available to go shopping, book tickets and carry out negotiations on a user’s behalf. The Facebook-owner’s app has been a hit in the US, where it is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, and has also launched in Canada and Australia. The assistant comes with a cuddly avatar as default, but users are invited to give it a name, look and a personality. Continue reading...

articles.title: Shop small, save big: 21 brilliant Black Friday bargains from UK independents
articles.description: From farm-to-table hot sauce to handwoven blankets, here are our favourite discounts from bricks-and-mortar shops and indie retailers • The best Black Friday deals Listen: we love a discounted air fryer as much as the next person, but there’s no doubt shopping for Black Friday deals can feel a bit … icky. From handing even more of your cash to global corporations to the suspicion you’re adding to a mass of plastic floating somewhere in the Antarctic, it’s no wonder a third of Britons say they hate Black Friday. But there is a way of having your discounted jacket and wearing it too. And that’s by shopping with local and independent retailers. Many wonderful bricks-and-mortar shops and small online retailers around the UK take part in Black Friday, often in creative and fun ways. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why is France fighting Vanuatu over two uninhabited islands in the Pacific?
articles.description: The battle over the Matthew and Hunter islands – and their 350,000 sq km economic zone – has made its way to the UN’s highest court Two tiny specks of volcanic land in the vast Pacific Ocean – home to seabirds and not much else – are at the centre of an escalating territorial battle between France and Vanuatu. The decades-long dispute over the Matthew and Hunter islands has entered a new phase, with Vanuatu launching two separate international legal proceedings against France as part of its attempt to claim these Pacific territories. Arbitration proceedings began last month, which could threaten France’s claim to a vast expanse of the ocean surrounding the islands. Continue reading...

articles.title: Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story
articles.description: After being longlisted twice before, Iqbal takes the award for unpublished short stories by writers of colour for a tale about a teenage female friendship Read Darkroom here Meher Iqbal has won this year’s 4thWrite prize for short fiction with her story Darkroom, after being longlisted twice in the past. The writer wins £1,000, publication of her story on the Guardian website, and a one-day workshop at the publisher 4th Estate. Darkroom traces the friendship between two teenage girls, Zara and Nadia, as they navigate the excitements and challenges of adolescence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Looking for a new laptop? The best Black Friday laptop deals in the UK, from Macbooks to budget Windows
articles.description: With RAM prices climbing, now is the perfect time to nab a discount. Here are the best so far on Acer, Chromebooks, gaming laptops and more • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals under £50 Looking for a new laptop this Black Friday? If you’re overdue an upgrade, there are some very real reasons to take advantage of these Black Friday laptop deals. The rise of AI has hit computing (and all consumer tech) hard. articles.title: Two men appear in court accused of stealing cufflinks and a clock from William and Kate's home
articles.description: Two men have appeared in court accused of stealing cufflinks and a clock from the Norfolk home of the Prince and Princess of Wales.

articles.title: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty
articles.description: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the event

articles.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
articles.description: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
articles.description: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.title: Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above
articles.description: The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse. He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. Any one of them could have pulled the trigger. Continue reading...

articles.title: Raheem Sterling avoids jail over reckless driving while using nitrous oxide
articles.description: He gets 12-month sentence suspended for 18 months Former England forward must do community service Raheem Sterling has avoided being sent to jail after he received a suspended sentence of 12 months for pleading guilty to a prolonged period of reckless driving while impaired by the drug nitrous oxide. The former England international, who five years ago was leading the Three Lions’ charge to a European Championship final, stood expressionless in the dock as the sentence was read out by district judge Kirsty Allman at Basingstoke magistrates court. Continue reading...

articles.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
articles.description: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024). Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
articles.description: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

articles.title: Still racist, misogynistic and homophobic. I’m putting Britain’s biggest police force on notice – we won’t tolerate this | Sadiq Khan
articles.description: Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most. Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
articles.description: We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely , especially if they’re young. The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking .) Continue reading...

articles.title: Bill McKibben: 2027 may be the year Americans turn on fossil fuels – Stateside with Kai and Carter
articles.description: It’s been another year in which the climate emergency has encroached on the lives of Americans across the country. From gigantic waves battering the California coastline to heat domes driving triple-digit temperatures in the southwest, we are reminded regularly that a crisis is here. Meanwhile, leaders gathered in Turkey for Cop31 failed to reach an agreement on how to move forward, and the US didn’t even bother to show up. To understand this moment, Kai Wright speaks to the environmentalist and author Bill McKibben about what he thinks must be done to slow the rapid advances of global heating, and what he wants to see from Democrats in 2027. Plus, he answers your questions about solar power, and how to talk to your family about the climate emergency Continue reading...

articles.title: Dolphins with active social lives and big friendship groups live longer, Australian researchers discover
articles.description: Decades of data collected at WA’s Shark Bay shows level of socialising may affect longevity for Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins Dolphins who spend time socialising in large and consistently sized social groups tend to live longer, new research has found. Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins are marine mammals that can live for more than 50 years and have complex social lives. They spend time socialising in groups – which increase in size during their youth and early adulthood, before declining towards the end of their life, according to a study in PLOS Biology. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Continue reading...

articles.title: M&G boss urges UK to stem flood of firms leaving London Stock Exchange after Compass exit

articles.title: EasyJet boss unable to rule out further job losses after profits collapse by 96%

EasyJet’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
articles.description: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evo

articles.title: Post your questions for Danny Boyle
articles.description: The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting. Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music with plans to delete more than 27m tracks
articles.description: Streaming service says 43% of uploads to platform in past 90 days were made entirely by artificial intelligence The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”. “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday. articles.description: Swap your kitchen island for a disco ball and ditch the dill, because blood sausages and burnt honey are in … Salt bread The Korean bakery icon, also known as sogeum-ppang , is made by wrapping pillow-soft bread dough around a baton of cold salted butter, to create a golden-crisp bottom and airy-tender inside as it bakes. articles.title: Christmas means chocolate – here are my top picks
articles.description: Whether you want the comfort of a traditional festive wreath or something much more startling (I’m talking goat’s cheese and sweet potato jam), I’ve got you covered This time of year is complex. A combination of sadness, joy, loss and acquisition. Winter leaves shed and transform into apricot-gold carpets; we don layers against the cold and the dark; and we wait for Christmas, and a slide into its tinselly, twinkly embrace. Bears have it right with hibernation but then, who would eat all the crumble? I have some ideas for chocolate things you might like: for you or to give to those who deserve it. articles.title: Venison stew and cod with celeriac and lentils: Chris and Jeff Galvin’s recipes for winter warmers
articles.description: These hearty and comforting dishes will keep the chill at bay It’s a big year for us: not only are we celebrating 15 years of holding a Michelin star at Galvin La Chapelle in Spitalfields, London, our country pub, Galvin Green Man near Chelmsford in Essex, has turned 10. Hearty, generous and rooted in classic technique, both capture exactly what we stand for. Continue reading...

articles.title: Which gaming headsets are worth the cost? I put 20 to the test – here are the best for 2026
articles.description: Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming • The best gaming chairs We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important. Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies. articles.title: Poundland collapses, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.description: Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza. The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Continue reading...

articles.title: Judge orders transfer of Thomas Markle to face formal charges in California

articles.title: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

articles.title: Lammens errors cost Manchester United victory in frantic finale at Sporting
articles.description: “We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then watched Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama every time they lace up their boots. Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez equalised with a bicycle kick. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent winner only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the official ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu. articles.title: Woman did not believe husband had drugged her for rape by strangers, Manchester trial told
articles.description: Wife said to detectives: ‘I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true’ A woman who was allegedly raped and sexually assaulted by men her husband invited to their home after he drugged her told police she could not believe it happened. In a video interview played to a jury at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, she told detectives: “I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true, and I think you have made a mistake.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath
articles.description: Images of Dimorphos four years on from crash could help scientists design potential planetary defence system Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter. Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists have released the first closeup images of the aftermath. Continue reading...

articles.title: Max Balegde: how influencer turned a cunning comms plan into a No 10 nightmare
articles.description: Backlash to a single video overshadows Andy Burnham’s attempt to connect with hard-to-reach audiences When excited content creators gathered in the opulent surroundings of 10 Downing Street earlier this month, their mingling and poses in front of a Glambot camera were interrupted by a warm welcome from the prime minister. After showing the 60 or so gathered content creators a video of his own Instagram reel bloopers, Andy Burnham explained that he too had faced criticism for his prolific social media content. But, said the enthusiastic member of the creator ranks, he would continue because he was trying to reach people “where they were at”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Raheem Sterling’s rise and fall: a sign football is broken? - The Latest
articles.description: Raheem Sterling has been handed a 12-month jail term, suspended for 18 months, for reckless driving and possession of nitrous oxide. It marks a remarkable fall from grace for the former England and Manchester City player, who was awarded an MBE in 2021. Sterling started playing professional football at 16, and his sentencing has raised questions about whether there are sufficient protections for younger players. articles.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
articles.description: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Vanity Fair’s takedown of Taylor Swift illuminating – or just a lot of hot air? | Arwa Mahdawi

An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape. To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett , was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the

articles.title: The bathroom’s wrecked, I’m soaked – but at long last the dog is clean | Adrian Chiles
articles.description: ‘It’s the washing he doesn’t like,’ said the dog groomer sagely. Talk about an understatement He knew what was coming. I don’t hold with the idea of dogs being super-clever. All the bum-sniffing, squirrel-chasing and obsession with balls and sticks suggest otherwise. But on this occasion my dog was on the money. I know this, because he disappeared. We’d got in, mid-afternoon, and I’d put the bath on. The dog groomer was coming later, you see – though with my dog it’s more about shearing than grooming. What the job really demands is a bare-chested Aussie sheep-shearing champion, but there are none advertised in my area. Continue reading...

articles.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
articles.description: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the Ame

articles.title: They’re bringing sexy back – but this time it’s classy | Jess Cartner-Morley
articles.description: From a V-neck sweater worn back-to-front to a perfectly framed collarbone – here’s the secret to low-stakes sex appeal I’m not sure when it started being not chic to want to look sexy, but it’s definitely a thing and it bothers me as it doesn’t feel truthful to the human experience, if that’s not a lot for the first sentence of a fashion column. Our wardrobes have become shrines to good taste. Well-cut coats and quality knitwear, elegant flat shoes and crisp white shirts. These clothes are excellent at communicating that you have read the briefing notes for the meeting and have some Booker prize chat. They are less good at suggesting you might be up for dancing on a table later. Why do we have to choose? Clothes have always been partly about how they make us feel physically. We accept that an outfit can make you feel powerful, cool, smart. Why shouldn’t it also make you feel hot and fun? Continue reading...

articles.description: The guitarist was absolutely integral to Duran Duran’s success, and not merely because he was by far the band’s most straightforwardly talented musician Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65 It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music. Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose. The joint statement was issued on Wednesday in response to a Ukrainian report circulated ​to 193 countries as the Organisation ‌for the Prohibition of Chemical ‌Weapons (OPCW) gathered in The Hague this week. The OPCW said “designated laboratories” approved by the watchdog had “confirmed the presence of a riot-control agent (CS) in samples ​collected at the scene”.
